name: Beth Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a packaging line at Elmbrook, a plant that packs medicines for drug companies. My line takes tablets, seals them into blister packs, those plastic-and-foil strips, folds them into cartons with the leaflet, and checks every single one with cameras. I've got six people and one cobot, which is a collaborative robot, the small kind that works next to people without a cage. Most days I'm chasing line stops, checking batch records and keeping the auditors happy, because in pharma one wrong leaflet can mean a recall.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you get on with the tech side of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love it, honestly. I use AI every day, I paste in the line-stop log at the end of shift and ask it what's causing the most downtime, and I use it to draft work instructions in plain words. I was the one who pushed for the cobot on the cartoner, and I set up its first program with the integrator. At home it's me and my partner Sam, he's a chef, so we basically meet at midnight, and we've got about five months of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, so the boring one. I'd be a bit surprised, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a good tool and not a miracle. I'd still be posting little wins on the line, like when AI found that a sensor bracket was loose and causing half our stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it would barely touch me. I'd keep using it as a sharp assistant, and I'd still be pushing for more cobots because they're good for us, nobody wants to lift cartons for eight hours. My career would carry on at a normal pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, keep using AI for the line, and push to get a second cobot on the case packer within a year. Savings carry on about the same. Maybe I'd do a short course in automation because I'd enjoy it, not because I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little bit let down, like a gig that's fine but not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody wants to lift cartons all day. Did the cobot take someone's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that matters to me. It took the part of Lena's job that was wrecking her wrists, and she moved to the camera checks. She was nervous at first. Now she calls it 'the intern' and tells it off when it drops a carton.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about this version that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people might stop taking the tools seriously because the hype burst. The useful stuff doesn't stop being useful just because the headlines get bored.

S0.say: She'd say AI is a good tool rather than a miracle, and keep posting small wins from the line, like the loose bracket it helped find.
S0.think: She thinks it would barely affect her and she'd keep using AI as an assistant while pushing for more cobots to spare people heavy lifting. Her career would carry on normally.
S0.do: Keeps going and keeps using AI on the line, pushing for a second cobot on the case packer within a year. Considers a short automation course for interest, with savings unchanged.
S0.feel: Calm and a little let down, like a fine but unremarkable gig.
S0.quote: She was nervous at first. Now she calls it 'the intern' and tells it off when it drops a carton.
S0.fieldNote: Beth is genuinely enthusiastic about tools and has already brought automation onto her line. She is careful to point out it spared a colleague's wrists rather than taking her job. Even in the fizzle she sees AI as useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more or less how I see things going. This one feels real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who learn the new kit will be fine, and companies need to help everyone else learn it. No point pretending it isn't happening. I'd say that in team meetings and I'd be the one running the sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is good for me. There'll be a lot more robots on lines, and not many people who understand both the line and the robot. That's me. I'd honestly expect a promotion out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up to lead the next automation project at Elmbrook in the first few months. I'd do a proper robot programming certificate, the kind that takes a few weekends, and I'd train my team on the AI tools. Savings carry on, maybe a bit more if a promotion came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. A bit worried for some of my team, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe. He's been on blister lines for fifteen years, he's careful and steady, and he hates anything with a screen. I'd sit with him and show him things slowly. Some people just need someone who won't make them feel stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave Elmbrook in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a robot integrator offered me a lot more money, yes, probably. I'm loyal, but I'm not naive. I'd give Elmbrook the first chance though.

S1.say: She'd say people who learn the new kit will be fine and companies must help the rest learn too. She'd say it in team meetings and run the training herself.
S1.think: She believes it's good for her, since few people understand both production lines and robots. She'd expect a promotion.
S1.do: Volunteers to lead the next automation project within months and takes a weekend robot programming certificate. Trains her team on AI tools and keeps saving.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, with some worry for team members.
S1.quote: Some people just need someone who won't make them feel stupid.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like opportunity to Beth, and she'd actively bring more automation in. She thinks practically about helping colleagues like Joe rather than about policy. She is open about leaving for more money but feels loyalty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's when even I'd sit up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be messy and governments need to get some kind of income support moving fast. I'd also say, to anyone who'd listen, learn whatever you can right now, because the people who are useful during the switch will be fine for a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I've got maybe a two- or three-year window where I'm really valuable, installing and fixing the robots. After that, if the AI can program the robots itself, I'm in the same boat as everyone. Five months of savings feels very thin when you think about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd move to a robot integrator, where they'd pay me more for knowing pharma lines. I'd save every bit of the extra money, aiming for a full year of expenses. I'd also do freelance weekend setups for small packing firms, to get a second income while the demand's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a driven way. I'd be busy, not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we might need to lean on his wage later, and on mine now. He'd ask whether restaurants would be okay. I'd say people will always want someone to cook for them, and I'd mean it about half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'fine for a bit longer'. What happens after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd hope the money goes somewhere sensible, but I'm not naive about it. That's why I'd save like mad while I could.

S2.say: She'd say it will be messy and governments must move fast on income support. She'd urge people to learn whatever they can now to stay useful during the transition.
S2.think: She sees a two- to three-year window where installing and fixing robots makes her valuable, after which she'd be like everyone else. Five months of savings would feel thin.
S2.do: Moves to a robot integrator within six months for higher pay and saves it towards a year of expenses. Takes freelance weekend setup work for small packing firms as a second income.
S2.feel: Anxious but driven and busy rather than frozen.
S2.quote: I'd say people will always want someone to cook for them, and I'd mean it about half.
S2.fieldNote: Even Beth's optimism has limits in the fast version: she sees her advantage as a short window. Her response is to earn and save hard while demand lasts. She is honest about not knowing what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to be properly ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain a lot of people if companies get on with it. I'd be pushing Elmbrook to start now, and I'd volunteer to help design the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think five years puts me in a good spot. I could become an automation engineer, not just an operator who knows robots. After 2031, who knows, but I'd be closer to the people deciding things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time automation engineering course in year one, about two evenings a week for two years. Around year three I'd move into an integrator role or an engineering job at Elmbrook. I'd save harder, aiming for eight or nine months of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly positive, but there's always that question at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'closer to the people deciding things' mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means being in the meeting where they decide which line gets automated and how, instead of finding out from the noticeboard. If I'm in that room, I can at least say, give Joe six months and some training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry you'd be seen as part of the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Someone already called me 'robot Beth' in the canteen. But if it's coming anyway, I'd rather it was done by someone who knows the people on the line.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to retrain many people if companies act. She'd push her plant to start now and volunteer to help design training.
S3.think: She thinks five years lets her become an automation engineer and be closer to decisions. She admits not knowing what comes after 2031.
S3.do: Starts a two-year part-time automation engineering course in year one and moves into an integrator or engineering role around year three. Saves harder towards eight or nine months of expenses.
S3.feel: Uneasy, mostly positive but with a question at the end.
S3.quote: Someone already called me 'robot Beth' in the canteen.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Beth plans a step up into engineering, wanting a seat where automation decisions are made. She accepts being seen as part of the change and argues it's better done by someone who knows the workers. Her unease is about the end point rather than the path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. I like the sound of that one, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get it right. Train people, plan for it, don't panic. I'd say it at work and I'd mean every word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me personally, ten years is great. I could build a real career in automation. What bothers me is what's left once even that is done by machines. That's a bigger question than my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the automation engineering course over two or three years, part-time, without rushing. I'd look at putting some savings into a small share of the integrator firm if they offered it to staff, or into an index fund. I'd keep going at Elmbrook in the meantime and keep leading the cobot projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Good for me, but I can't quite picture what my thirties look like at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why invest rather than just save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in this version, the money goes to whoever owns the machines. If I can own even a tiny bit, I'm on the right side of that. Sam laughs at me for reading investing forums at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably think about kids around thirty-two, thirty-three. Ten years makes that feel normal. Two years wouldn't.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty to get it right through training and planning without panic, and she'd mean it.
S4.think: She sees ten years as great for building a career in automation. What bothers her is what's left when machines do even that work.
S4.do: Studies automation engineering part-time over two or three years. Considers buying a small staff share in the integrator firm or putting savings into an index fund, while continuing to lead cobot projects at her plant.
S4.feel: Uneasy: good for her career but hard to picture the end of her thirties.
S4.quote: If I can own even a tiny bit, I'm on the right side of that.
S4.fieldNote: Beth's long-horizon plan combines retraining with buying a small stake in automation. Her unease is philosophical rather than financial. The long timeline lets her think about children in a normal way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everyone would be scrambling at once, me included, and the people who can't scramble get left. What would help is income support that kicks in fast, and companies being required to give people real training time, paid, not just a login to an online course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we're excited about. Everyone asks about fear. I'm excited too. Both things are true, and it's weird to hold them at the same time.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about fear. I'm excited too. Both things are true, and it's weird to hold them at the same time.
portrait: Beth Ibrahim is twenty-seven, a line lead at a pharmaceutical packaging plant, living with her partner Sam, a chef, with about five months of savings. She uses AI every day and pushed for the cobot on her own line, which she points out spared a colleague's wrists. She is calm when AI fizzles and with steady change, where she would lead automation projects and expect promotion. AGI in two years makes her anxious, because she sees only a short window of value, and she would jump to an integrator and save hard. With five or ten years she plans an engineering career and a small stake in automation, uneasy mainly about what remains once machines do that too.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because everyone would be scrambling at once and those who can't would be left behind.
whatWouldHelp: Fast income support and companies being required to give workers real, paid training time.
